elements.texte:
[cheerful] For every order, the warehouse prints a shipping label for each parcel.

To make the carrier’s job easier, we’ll put the last name, address and city in capitals.

Example: for Sophie Martin, the label reads MARTIN Sophie, 12, rue des Lilas, Paris.

The street number has its own box, next to the address.

To print, get the last name, first name, address and city of the 10 customers in the customers table.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To bring two texts together in a single column, we join them with two vertical bars.

In between, we add a space, written between single quotes.

Result: MARTIN Sophie, just like on the label.

Careful: with the plus sign instead of two vertical bars, the query returns 0.

So to join texts, always use two vertical bars, never the plus sign.

[cheerful] Lower does the opposite of upper: it puts everything in lowercase.

Trim removes the spaces at the start and end of a text.

Length counts the characters: the first name Sophie has 6.

Substring of last underscore name, 1, 3 gets the first 3 characters of the last name.

Replace lets you replace characters in a text.

Here, it removes the spaces from the phone number.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To split off the street number, we need to know where it ends: at the first space.

In-string of address, space gives the position of that first space: 3.

Substring keeps the characters before that space, so 3 minus 1 equals 2: 12.

The plus 1 lets us start just after the first space.

With no length given, substring extracts all the remaining text: “rue des Lilas”.
